goal.outcome: Close on a main-street business (HVAC, services, or light manufacturing) within 12 months using an SBA 7(a) loan with a 10/10/80 financing structure, having completed full diligence and negotiated a defined seller transition.
constraints: SBA 7(a) minimum 10% equity injection required — up to half can be a seller note on full standby
SBA lender requires DSCR ≥ 1.25× after buyer salary
Unlimited personal guarantee required for all owners with 20%+ stake
success: Pre-qualified with at least one SBA preferred lender with a target deal size range in hand
LOI signed on a business with verified SDE and a DSCR ≥ 1.25×
Quality of earnings report completed before contingencies removed
Seller transition period of 90+ days negotiated into the APA
First 90 days post-close executed without revenue loss from the transition

approach.recommended: SBA 7(a) with seller note — 10% cash equity, 10% seller note on full standby, 80% SBA loan. Target main-street businesses at 2.0×–3.5× SDE with verified earnings via a quality of earnings report before removing contingencies.
approach.why: This is the dominant, lender-validated structure for this asset class. Seller note on standby cuts actual cash needed to 5% of purchase price (e.g., $50K on a $1M deal), the 10-year term and government guarantee make rates and terms accessible, and the lender's DSCR floor acts as a built-in overpayment guard. HVAC and services businesses are exactly the 'boring businesses' that SBA lenders know and brokers transact regularly, reducing friction.

alternatives.why_not: Sellers willing to carry 100% of a note are rare, especially in attractive sectors like HVAC. Without a lender's DSCR check you become your own underwriter with no safety net. Treat as a fallback for a uniquely motivated seller, not a primary strategy.

alternatives.option: Target managed businesses at 3.5×–4× SDE to offset lack of industry experience
alternatives.why_not: Valid if operator experience is a real lender concern, but higher multiples require more cash at close and push the timeline to 12–18 months. Revisit only if lenders flag your background as a qualification risk.

first_steps.action: Total your liquid capital today — every non-retirement, accessible account.
first_steps.detail: The SBA requires a minimum 10% equity injection. Up to half (5% of purchase price) can come from a seller note on full standby, so your true minimum cash floor is 5% of the deal size you want to pursue. You cannot size a deal, pick a lender, or model DSCR until you know this number. Write it down.

first_steps.action: Call two SBA Preferred Lenders (PLP status) this week and ask for a pre-qualification conversation.
first_steps.detail: Tell them: your liquid capital, that you're targeting a main-street business acquisition (HVAC / services / light manufacturing), and ask what deal size they'd support and what they need from you. This is free. It gives you a real deal-size ceiling and starts the lender relationship you'll need later.

first_steps.action: Write your target criteria on one page: geography, sectors (rank them), revenue range, minimum SDE, must-have operational characteristics (e.g., does not require owner to be a licensed technician).
first_steps.detail: This single document prevents you from spending 6+ months looking at everything. It also tells brokers exactly what to send you, which improves the quality of deal flow immediately.

phases.name: Phase 1 — Qualify & Set Criteria (Weeks 1–4)
phases.objective: Know your deal size, have at least one lender pre-qual conversation on record, and have written target criteria that you're actively sharing with brokers.

tasks.task: Calculate exact liquid capital and source-of-funds documentation
tasks.detail: Bank statements, brokerage statements, any gift letters if family capital is involved. Lenders will verify every dollar of equity injection.

tasks.task: Contact 2–3 SBA Preferred Lenders for pre-qualification
tasks.detail: Focus on lenders with active acquisition lending desks — community banks and credit unions with SBA PLP status close faster than large national banks. Ask specifically about their acquisition experience in your target sectors.

tasks.task: Write and finalize one-page target criteria document
tasks.detail: Geography, sector priority, revenue $500K–$5M (adjust to your capital), SDE floor (run the deal calculator to find the SDE needed to clear 1.25× DSCR at your expected deal size), owner-involvement level acceptable.

tasks.task: Identify and contact 5–8 business brokers active in your target geography and sectors
tasks.detail: Register on BizBuySell and ask brokers you contact to add you to their VIP buyer list. Most deals worth buying are shown to preferred buyers before hitting public listings.

tasks.task: Engage a buy-side M&A attorney for an introductory conversation
tasks.detail: You don't need to retain yet, but identify who you'll call when an LOI is needed. Look for attorneys who have closed SBA-financed acquisitions — they know the lender's requirements and will draft the APA accordingly.

decisions: What deal size range to target
phases.outcome: Pre-qualification letter or conversation in hand; broker relationships started; deal size ceiling confirmed.

phases.name: Phase 2 — Structured Search (Months 2–7)
phases.objective: Generate and evaluate a pipeline of deals against your criteria. Move quickly to LOI on the first business that clears a preliminary financial screen.

tasks.task: Maintain a weekly outreach cadence — minimum 5 broker touches per week
tasks.detail: Track in a simple spreadsheet: broker name, date, deal, status. Cadence beats volume — consistent follow-up is how you get deals before they're marketed widely.

tasks.task: For every CIM received, run a 15-minute preliminary DSCR screen before reading further
tasks.detail: Use the deal calculator structure: (SDE – your salary) ÷ estimated annual debt service ≥ 1.25. If it fails at the asking price, the business either needs a lower price or is not for you. Do this before you get emotionally invested.

tasks.task: Visit businesses that clear the preliminary screen — meet the owner, see the operation
tasks.detail: You're assessing customer concentration, owner dependence, and key employee risk in person. These are not discoverable from a CIM alone.

tasks.task: Submit LOI on the first business that clears your screen and site visit
tasks.detail: LOI should state the purchase price, the SDE figure you're basing it on (so there's no later dispute), deal structure (10/10/80), exclusivity period (60 days minimum for SBA diligence), and a defined transition period requirement. Keep it non-binding except for exclusivity and confidentiality.

decisions: When to submit LOI vs. keep searching
Whether seller note on standby is achievable with this seller
phases.outcome: Signed LOI with exclusivity period on a business that has passed preliminary financial screening.

phases.name: Phase 3 — Diligence (Months 6–9, ~60–90 days after LOI)
phases.objective: Verify the SDE number is real, confirm no legal/operational landmines, and get SBA lender to credit approval.

tasks.task: Commission a Quality of Earnings report immediately after LOI is signed
tasks.detail: Cost: $8K–$20K for a business under $5M revenue. The QoE ties tax returns to bank statements and stress-tests every add-back. Apply the strict test: does this expense genuinely disappear when the seller leaves? If QoE reduces SDE by more than 15%, renegotiate price or walk.

tasks.task: Request and review the lease on day one of diligence
tasks.detail: Confirm remaining term (want 5+ years or renewal options), assignment clause, and landlord consent requirement. A non-assignable lease with 18 months remaining is a deal-killer. Your SBA lender will also require this.

tasks.task: Verify customer concentration — top 10 customers as % of revenue
tasks.detail: A single customer over 20% of revenue is a significant risk. Over 30% will concern your lender and should concern you. Ask for 3 years of revenue by customer.

tasks.task: Confirm key employee plans — interview lead technicians or operators (with seller permission)
tasks.detail: In HVAC and services, the lead tech often is the business. Ask seller to facilitate introductions. Consider structuring retention bonuses (6–12 months of salary) funded from the deal.

tasks.task: Submit formal SBA loan application to your pre-qualified lender
tasks.detail: Provide QoE report, 3 years tax returns, seller's financial statements, lease, and your personal financial statement. Budget 60–90 days for SBA credit approval and closing.

tasks.task: Have your attorney draft and negotiate the Asset Purchase Agreement
tasks.detail: Key provisions: working capital peg (normal level of receivables + inventory – payables that seller must deliver at close), representations and warranties, non-compete (minimum 3–5 years in same geography and sector), and seller transition period (90–180 days).

decisions: Whether to proceed after QoE results
phases.outcome: SBA credit approval, signed APA, and a confirmed closing date.

phases.name: Phase 4 — Close & First 90 Days (Months 9–12)
phases.objective: Close cleanly, protect revenue during the ownership handoff, and stabilize operations.

tasks.task: Confirm equity injection funds are in place and sourced 30 days before close
tasks.detail: Lender will verify source of funds. Do not move money around in the 60 days before closing without telling your lender — unexplained transfers create underwriting problems.

tasks.task: Execute seller transition plan: shadow the owner for weeks 1–4, take the lead in weeks 5–8, solo in weeks 9+
tasks.detail: Introduce yourself to key customers and employees in person during the transition period. Revenue risk is highest in the first 60 days — your presence and the seller's endorsement are the best mitigation.

tasks.task: Don't change anything in the first 30 days — observe before you optimize
tasks.detail: Operational changes in week one destroy employee trust and customer relationships. Your job in month one is to learn how the business actually runs, not how the CIM said it runs.

tasks.task: Set up financial reporting: weekly P&L vs. prior year, accounts receivable aging, cash balance
tasks.detail: The single most important operational tool is knowing your numbers weekly, not monthly. You need to catch a revenue shortfall in week 3, not month 3.

decisions: Who manages day-to-day in weeks 1–4 if seller is less available than agreed
phases.outcome: Business closed, ownership transferred, revenue stable at or above pre-close run rate at day 90.

dependencies.note: Nothing else can be sized or modeled without this number. Do it today.
Required before submitting an LOI — you need to know the lender will fund the deal size you're targeting.
Never remove diligence contingencies without it. Non-negotiable even on small deals.
A non-assignable lease kills the deal at close or creates catastrophic post-close risk.

dependencies.item: Seller's acceptance of standby seller note
dependencies.note: If seller refuses standby terms, you need the full 10% in cash rather than 5%. Know this before modeling.

decisions.decision: What deal size range to target
decisions.recommended: Match to your liquid capital: minimum cash floor is 5% of purchase price if seller note is achievable, 10% if not.
decisions.why: The SBA equity injection requirement is a hard constraint. Targeting above your capital floor is not viable.

decisions.decision: Sector priority within HVAC / services / light manufacturing
options: HVAC — strong recurring revenue, PE rollup tailwinds on exit, requires licensed technicians
Commercial cleaning / landscaping — lower multiples, more substitutable workforce, easier to operate
Light manufacturing — asset-heavy, SBA real estate loan possible (25-year term), requires operational knowledge
decisions.recommended: HVAC or services if you want recurring revenue and a proven SBA deal type. Light manufacturing only if you have relevant operational background.
decisions.why: Lenders and brokers know HVAC and services well. Light manufacturing has higher operational complexity for an inexperienced buyer.

decisions.decision: Seller note standby negotiation — raise it early or late in the process
options: Include standby seller note requirement in the LOI (transparent, may lose some sellers)
Negotiate after LOI acceptance (more flexibility, but risk of surprise at the lender stage)
decisions.recommended: Include it in the LOI. Sellers who refuse standby terms need to be identified before you spend $8K–$20K on diligence.
decisions.why: If the seller won't accept standby, your equity injection requirement doubles. This changes your deal math fundamentally.

upfront.item: Equity injection — cash portion (5–10% of purchase price)
SBA loan origination fee (included in loan, often financed)

recurring.item: SBA loan payment (80% of purchase price at ~10.5% over 10 years)
recurring.amount: ~$10,700/month on $800K loan — model with deal calculator

services.amount: No direct fee; loan fees financed into deal

services.item: Business broker (seller-paid, typically 10–12% of deal price)

costs.contingency: Budget 10–15% above your professional fee estimates for surprises — unexpected legal complexity, a second round of lender documentation, or a renegotiation after the QoE.
costs.minimum: $63,000 all-in on a $1M deal (5% cash injection + QoE + attorney at low end)
costs.recommended: $100,000 all-in on a $1M deal (10% full cash injection + QoE + attorney at mid-range + contingency)
costs.premium: $135,000+ if seller won't accept standby and you need full 10% cash plus advisor
costs.note: These are deal-closing costs only. Ensure you retain 3–6 months of personal living expenses outside of the equity injection — the SBA lender may verify this as part of your personal financial statement.

risks.risk: Add-back inflation overstates SDE — you pay too much and DSCR fails post-QoE
risks.mitigation: Commission QoE before removing contingencies. Apply strict add-back test: does this expense disappear when the seller leaves? Renegotiate price if QoE reduces SDE by more than 10–15%.

risks.risk: Search drags past month 7, leaving insufficient time to close within 12 months
risks.mitigation: Set a written weekly activity target (5 broker contacts, 2 CIM reviews). Use the preliminary DSCR screen to kill bad deals fast and avoid emotional attachment. Submit an LOI on the first business that clears your criteria — don't wait for perfect.

risks.risk: Lease is non-assignable or expires within 24 months of close
risks.mitigation: Request the lease on day one of diligence. If landlord consent is required, start that conversation immediately — landlords can delay or kill deals at the last minute.

risks.risk: Key technician or operator leaves at or after close, destroying revenue
risks.mitigation: Interview key employees during diligence. Negotiate employment agreements or retention bonuses into the APA. A 90–180 day seller transition provides cover while you assess and secure the team.

risks.risk: Seller refuses standby terms, requiring full 10% cash injection
risks.mitigation: Surface this in the LOI negotiation before spending on diligence. If seller refuses standby, re-model deal with full 10% cash — proceed only if you have it.

gotchas.gotcha: The SBA process takes 60–90 days from application to close — sellers who want speed will choose cash or seller-financed buyers over you.
gotchas.avoid: Get pre-qualified with a lender BEFORE you find a deal. A lender who already knows your file can move in 45 days instead of 90. Tell sellers and brokers you are pre-qualified — it matters.

gotchas.gotcha: Moving money around in the 60 days before closing triggers lender re-underwriting. Unexplained deposits or transfers can delay or kill closing.
gotchas.avoid: Keep your equity injection funds in a stable, documented account from the moment you submit the LOI. Tell your lender before moving anything.

gotchas.gotcha: The LOI is where working capital is either protected or lost — most first-time buyers skip the working capital peg, then discover the seller drained receivables before close.
gotchas.avoid: Include a working capital peg in the LOI: a defined 'normal' level of net working capital that the seller must deliver at close. Your attorney should draft this — don't do it yourself.

gotchas.gotcha: A non-compete without geographic and time specificity is unenforceable in most states. A seller who reopens next door destroys the value you paid for.
gotchas.avoid: Have your attorney draft the non-compete with explicit geography (county or radius), duration (3–5 years), and scope (same services). Review with local counsel — enforceability varies by state.

gotchas.gotcha: Buying 'the business' but not securing the real estate can leave you at a landlord's mercy at renewal. In service businesses, location is often not critical, but in manufacturing, it frequently is.
gotchas.avoid: For manufacturing especially, confirm lease terms before the LOI. If real estate is included in the deal, the SBA loan can extend to 25 years — a meaningful improvement in cash flow.

defer.item: Deciding between HVAC vs. services vs. manufacturing
defer.until: After lender pre-qual conversation — lender may have sector preferences or restrictions
After 60 days of self-directed search — only add this cost if deal flow is genuinely insufficient

defer.item: Building detailed post-close operational plans for a specific business
defer.until: After LOI is signed — before that, it's premature and a distraction
Phase 2, when you're actively making offers — consult your attorney on optimal structure for the SBA loan

open_questions.question: What is your total liquid capital available for an equity injection, excluding retirement accounts?
open_questions.why: This single number determines every deal size you can pursue. Until it's known, no deal can be responsibly modeled.
open_questions.research_prompt: Total every non-retirement liquid account (checking, savings, brokerage, money market). Then ask your SBA lender: 'Given $X in liquid capital and a willingness to accept a seller note on standby for up to 5% of the deal, what purchase price range will you pre-qualify me for?'

open_questions.question: Do you have relevant operator or industry experience in HVAC, services, or manufacturing — and have you disclosed this to a lender?
open_questions.why: SBA lenders assess repayment ability partly through borrower background. Inexperienced buyers may face a higher required injection or need to demonstrate a management plan. Knowing this now shapes your search criteria.
open_questions.research_prompt: In your lender pre-qualification conversation, ask directly: 'I have [X years / no experience] in this sector — does that affect your required equity injection or your willingness to lend on this deal type?'

open_questions.question: Will you be operating the business full-time yourself, or do you need a business with an existing manager in place?
open_questions.why: Owner-operator businesses trade at 2–3× SDE but require your full-time involvement. Businesses with management in place trade at 3–4× SDE but work with an absentee buyer. This shapes your entire search.
open_questions.research_prompt: Decide before you start talking to brokers. Brokers will ask. A confused answer signals an unprepared buyer and reduces deal flow quality.

open_questions.question: What geography are you targeting — specific metro, state, or willing to relocate?
open_questions.why: Without a geography, your broker outreach list is undefined and search is impossible to structure. This is a decision only you can make.
open_questions.research_prompt: Write down your target geography in one sentence before your first broker call. Be specific enough to be actionable (e.g., 'Within 2 hours of Denver' or 'Southeast US, willing to relocate').

confidence.area: SBA financing mechanics (injection, standby, DSCR, guarantee)
confidence.note: Confirmed by program documentation and multiple practitioner sources.
2–3.5× SDE for sub-$1M earnings is consistent across sources. HVAC may trade higher due to PE interest.
Consistently flagged across sources as non-negotiable.

confidence.area: Your personal readiness (capital, experience, risk tolerance)
confidence.note: None of your personal financial details were provided. This is the single biggest unknown in the plan.
Achievable if search starts immediately and is structured. Search alone averages 6+ months. Slippage is a real risk.

Call two SBA Preferred Lenders this week for a pre-qualification conversation
Write your one-page target criteria (geography, sector, revenue range, SDE floor, operator role)
ready.initial_cost: $0 for pre-qualification conversations; $63K–$100K at deal close for equity injection and professional fees on a $1M deal
need_before: Target criteria written and shared with first broker
blockers: Unknown liquid capital — cannot size any deal until this is confirmed
No lender relationship — SBA pre-qualification is the longest lead-time item and must start now

this_week.action: Calculate and document your total liquid capital — print bank and brokerage statements, add them up, write the number down.
this_week.why: This is the single input that drives every other number in this plan. Without it you are guessing at deal sizes, DSCR math, and lender conversations.

this_week.action: Find and call two SBA Preferred Lenders (search 'SBA Preferred Lender Program' on SBA.gov for the lender directory). Tell them your liquid capital, your target sector, and ask what deal size they'd pre-qualify you for and what documentation they need.
this_week.why: Pre-qualification is the longest lead-time item in the whole process and it's free. Knowing your lender's ceiling before you start searching prevents wasted months pursuing deals you can't finance.

this_week.action: Write your one-page target criteria: geography (specific), sectors in priority order, revenue range, minimum SDE (calculate from deal calculator: what SDE do you need to clear 1.25× DSCR after your target salary?), and your role (full-time operator vs. absentee).
this_week.why: This document drives your entire broker outreach. Without it you receive random deal flow and evaluate everything, which leads to the six-month search trap.

this_week.action: Contact 5 business brokers active in your target geography: find them on BizBuySell broker directory or IBBA.org. Send a one-paragraph buyer profile (liquid capital range, sectors, deal size, timeline) and ask to be added to their off-market buyer list.
this_week.why: Most good deals are shown to preferred buyers before public listing. Getting on those lists early — even months before you're ready — is how you access real deal flow.

this_week.action: Run the deal calculator math at three price points ($750K, $1M, $1.5M): plug in 10% equity, 10% seller note, 80% SBA at 10.5% over 10 years, and your realistic salary. Confirm which price points clear 1.25× DSCR. Save the spreadsheet.
this_week.why: You need to be able to kill a bad deal in 15 minutes during the search phase. Having your DSCR thresholds pre-calculated prevents emotional attachment to deals that can't be financed.

refine_questions.question: How much liquid capital (non-retirement) do you have available right now for an equity injection?
refine_questions.why: This determines every deal size in the plan. A $50K answer means a very different search than a $200K answer. The entire financing structure, DSCR modeling, and lender conversations pivot on this number.

refine_questions.question: Do you have relevant work experience in HVAC, services, or manufacturing — and are you planning to operate the business full-time yourself?
refine_questions.why: Lenders assess borrower background for repayment ability. Your answer also determines whether you target owner-operator businesses (2–3× SDE, lower price) or managed businesses (3–4× SDE, higher price, less operator dependency).
options: No relevant experience — will operate full-time and learn on the job
No relevant experience — need a business with a manager already in place
Have relevant experience in [specific sector] and will operate full-time

refine_questions.question: What geography are you targeting — and are you willing to relocate for the right deal?
refine_questions.why: Without a geography, the broker outreach list and search process cannot be structured. This also affects lender choice (local lenders close acquisition deals faster than national banks in many markets).

refine_questions.question: How many hours per week can you realistically dedicate to this acquisition process right now, before you own anything?
refine_questions.why: A 12-month close is achievable at 10–15 hours/week of focused effort (search, broker calls, deal review). At 3–5 hours/week, the timeline is 18+ months. This changes whether the plan is realistic as written.

refine_questions.question: Have you internalized the personal guarantee — do you own a home, have retirement savings, or a spouse whose finances would be affected if the business failed?
refine_questions.why: Every owner with 20%+ must sign an unlimited personal guarantee on the SBA loan. This is not abstract. If you have not explicitly accepted this risk with full awareness of what's at stake, it needs to be resolved before you sign an LOI.
options: Yes, fully understood and accepted — proceed as planned
Partially understood — need to review with a financial advisor or spouse before proceeding
Not yet internalized — pause Phase 2 until resolved

analysis.situation: You are evaluating whether to buy a main-street business (HVAC, services, or light manufacturing) in the next 12 months using an SBA 7(a) loan as the primary financing vehicle. The goal is a fully formed decision — not just interest — including a clear financing structure, diligence checklist, and 90-day post-close plan. The research covers the core mechanics well: SBA equity injection rules, valuation multiples, diligence process, and deal structure. Your personal financial details (liquid capital, income, credit score, existing collateral) were not provided, which is the single biggest unknown in assessing your readiness right now.

strengths.point: Clear goal with a defined timeline (12 months to a decision)
strengths.so_what: You are not just browsing — having a hard deadline forces real action on search, financing pre-qualification, and diligence preparation rather than indefinite research loops.

strengths.point: Targeting the right asset class for SBA financing
strengths.so_what: HVAC, services, and light manufacturing are exactly the 'boring businesses' practitioners flag as most acquirable and most financeable under 7(a) — lenders and brokers know these categories well, reducing execution friction [C3].

strengths.point: You are asking the right starting questions (down payment, multiples, diligence killers)
strengths.so_what: These three questions map directly to the three biggest failure points in small business acquisition. Framing the problem correctly from the start saves months of misdirected effort.

weaknesses.so_what: The SBA requires a minimum 10% equity injection on a change-of-ownership loan [C4, C1]. On a $1M deal that is $100K cash at minimum — and up to half can be a seller note on full standby, meaning you still need $50K hard cash at minimum. Without knowing your liquid capital, no deal size can be responsibly modeled.

weaknesses.point: No stated operator experience in the target industries
weaknesses.so_what: SBA lenders assess 'repayment ability' partly through borrower background [C4]. An inexperienced buyer in HVAC or manufacturing may face a higher required equity injection or lender skepticism, and may underestimate operational complexity in the first 90 days.

weaknesses.point: No existing lender or broker relationships mentioned
weaknesses.so_what: Deal flow and lender pre-qualification are the two longest lead-time items. Starting without a preferred SBA lender or a broker relationship means you are 2–4 months behind someone who already has those in place.

weaknesses.point: Personal guarantee obligation not yet internalized
weaknesses.so_what: Every owner with 20%+ stake must sign an unlimited personal guarantee on the SBA loan [C4]. This puts personal assets at risk. If you have a home, retirement savings, or a spouse's assets, that exposure needs to be explicitly understood and accepted before signing an LOI.

opportunities.point: Seller note can cut actual cash needed in half
opportunities.so_what: Up to 5% of the purchase price (half the 10% injection) can come from a seller note on full standby, reducing your true out-of-pocket on a $1M deal from $100K to $50K [C1, C4]. This meaningfully expands the deal sizes you can pursue.

opportunities.point: Main-street businesses (2–3.5× SDE) are priced accessibly relative to lower-middle-market
opportunities.so_what: Businesses under $1M in SDE trade at 2.0×–3.5× SDE [C6, C12], making them reachable with SBA leverage. The math in the deal calculator shows a $1M purchase on $320K SDE yields a DSCR above 1.25 at current rates, which is the SBA minimum threshold [C5, C9].

opportunities.point: Working capital peg and LOI structure are well-understood and negotiable
opportunities.so_what: Standard deal architecture (10% equity / 10% seller note / 80% SBA, working capital peg, transition period) is documented and practiced — you are not inventing a structure, you are executing a known playbook [C8, C5, C14].

opportunities.point: HVAC and home services multiples are rising due to PE rollup activity
opportunities.so_what: As a buyer this is a threat on price, but it also signals strong exit potential if you ever sell. Buy at 3×, sell into a rollup at 5× is a realistic outcome in this sector [C2].

threats.point: Add-back inflation is the leading cause of paying too much
threats.so_what: Sellers routinely add back personal expenses (truck, phone, salary, one-time items) to inflate SDE. Without a quality of earnings report ($8K–$20K), you have no independent verification that the earnings number is real [C7]. Overpaying is the most common and most irreversible mistake.

threats.point: SBA process takes 60–90 days, creating deal fatigue and competition risk
threats.so_what: The paperwork timeline is real. A seller who wants to close fast may prefer a cash buyer or seller-financed deal over your SBA process. Pre-qualifying with a preferred SBA lender before you find a deal compresses this window significantly [C2].

threats.point: DSCR floor of 1.25× constrains price regardless of comparable sales
threats.so_what: Even if the market says 3.5× is fair, the lender will reject the deal if cash flow after your salary does not cover debt service at 1.25× [C5]. This acts as a hard ceiling on deal price for a given earnings level — model this before you fall in love with a business.

threats.point: Search phase drags on for 6–12+ months without a structured process
threats.so_what: Practitioners consistently describe buyers who spend 6–12 months searching and buy nothing [S1]. Without target criteria, a shortlist of brokers, and a weekly outreach cadence, the 12-month deadline will arrive with nothing to show.

readiness.note: Minimum 10% equity injection required by SBA, with up to half potentially covered by a seller note on full standby [C4, C1]. Your liquid capital figure is unknown. This is the first thing to nail down — it determines every deal size you can responsibly pursue. Get a bank statement total and talk to an SBA preferred lender for a pre-qualification letter before anything else.

You are asking the right questions, which puts you ahead of most first-time buyers. But knowing the framework and executing it (reading a quality of earnings report, negotiating a working capital peg, writing an LOI) are different skills. Plan to hire a buy-side M&A attorney and a CPA with acquisition experience — do not DIY those pieces.

No operator background was stated. For HVAC or light manufacturing, lenders and sellers will both probe this. Consider whether you are buying a business you will run yourself or one with a management team in place. The latter reduces lender concern but raises the price multiple [C6].

No existing relationships mentioned. Building a shortlist of 3–5 SBA preferred lenders and 5–10 active brokers in your target geography and sector is a month-one task. Deal flow comes from relationships, not just listing sites.

A 12-month horizon is realistic for a first acquisition if search starts immediately. Research shows search alone averages 6+ months [S1]. Diligence takes another 60–90 days. The timeline is tight but achievable if you treat this as a part-time second job from day one.

Unlimited personal guarantee [C4] and the reality of a 10-year SBA loan obligation need to be internalized, not just acknowledged. This is a leveraged bet on your ability to operate a business you have never run. The upside is real; so is the downside.

No mention of an entity structure, buy-side attorney, or familiarity with LOI / APA documents. These need to be in place before you make an offer. Attorney cost is typically $5K–$15K for a deal of this size — budget for it.

options.summary: Bring 5% cash, source 5% from a seller note on full standby, finance 80% via SBA 7(a) at prime + 2.5–3%. This is the standard playbook for main-street acquisitions and is explicitly validated by program rules and practitioners [C1, C4, C8]. On a $1M deal: $50K cash, $100K seller note (standby), $800K SBA loan at ~10.5% over 10 years ≈ $10.7K/month debt service. Requires SDE of roughly $223K+ after your salary to clear 1.25× DSCR [C9, C5].
options.cost: $50K–$100K cash at close (depending on seller note negotiation) plus $15K–$35K in professional fees (attorney, QoE, lender fees)
options.time_to_result: 6–12 months to close (search + 60–90 day SBA process)
options.why_fit: Matches the stated goal exactly. Maximizes leverage while keeping equity injection manageable. Seller note alignment (seller wants business to succeed so they get paid) is a structural bonus. This is the dominant structure for this asset class.

options.summary: Negotiate 100% seller financing over 5–7 years, paid from business cash flow. No SBA paperwork, no personal guarantee, no bank. Requires finding a highly motivated seller willing to carry the full note — typically a tired owner with no other buyers [C2, S3]. Valuation discipline matters even more here since there is no lender DSCR check acting as a floor.
options.cost: Near zero cash at close in the best case; seller may demand a larger down payment to offset risk
options.time_to_result: Potentially faster close (no bank process), but finding the right seller may take longer
options.why_fit: Theoretically attractive but hard to execute in practice. Sellers who will carry 100% are rare, especially in desirable sectors like HVAC. No lender DSCR discipline means you must be your own underwriter. The source citing this strategy [C2, S3] is a self-described contrarian who explicitly rejects SBA — treat as an edge case, not the base case.

options.path: Search longer, buy a managed business at 3.5–4× SDE
options.summary: Target a business with a management layer already in place — a general manager or lead tech who runs day-to-day operations — so you do not need deep industry experience. These businesses trade at the higher end of the multiple range (3–4× SDE) [C6] but carry lower operational risk for an inexperienced buyer. Still uses SBA financing but requires a larger deal (higher SDE) to absorb both the management cost and the debt service.
options.cost: Higher purchase price (larger equity injection) and longer search — likely 12–18 months total
options.why_fit: Better fit if you lack industry experience. Worse fit if you want to close within 12 months or have limited capital, since higher multiples require more cash at close.

options.path: Stay in research mode for 6 more months, then act
options.summary: Continue learning, build broker and lender relationships, shadow a deal as an advisor, and enter the market better prepared. Reduces execution risk but burns half the 12-month timeline.
options.cost: Minimal direct cost; opportunity cost of delay
options.why_fit: Lowest risk but conflicts directly with the stated goal of deciding within 12 months. The sources are clear that search alone takes 6–12 months [S1]. Delaying the start almost guarantees missing the deadline. Only choose this path if capital or personal guarantee concerns are not yet resolved.

assumptions.assumption: You have at least $50K–$100K in liquid capital available for an equity injection
assumptions.if_wrong: You cannot qualify for SBA 7(a) on a deal of any meaningful size without it. The program requires a minimum 10% injection and the lender will verify source of funds [C4].
assumptions.how_to_check: Total your liquid, non-retirement accounts today. Then call 2–3 SBA preferred lenders and ask for a pre-qualification conversation — they will tell you the deal size range you can support.

assumptions.assumption: The target business's SDE is real and will survive diligence
assumptions.if_wrong: Add-back inflation is the most common way deals fall apart or buyers overpay [C7]. If the QoE report reduces SDE by 20–30%, your DSCR may drop below 1.25× and the deal dies or requires renegotiation.
assumptions.how_to_check: Always commission a quality of earnings report ($8K–$20K) before removing diligence contingencies [C7, S4]. Never waive this.

assumptions.assumption: A seller in your target sector will accept 10% seller note on full standby
assumptions.if_wrong: If the seller refuses standby terms, the seller note cannot count toward your equity injection [C1, C4], and you need the full 10% in cash.
assumptions.how_to_check: Raise this early in seller conversations and in the LOI. Many sellers prefer a faster close over a larger note — some will not agree to standby. Know this before you model the deal.

assumptions.assumption: Business cash flow after your salary clears 1.25× DSCR on the proposed loan
assumptions.if_wrong: The SBA lender will decline or require a lower loan amount, forcing a price reduction or a larger equity injection [C5].
assumptions.how_to_check: Run the deal calculator math [C9] with realistic salary assumptions before making an offer. If DSCR < 1.25×, either negotiate a lower price or walk away.

assumptions.assumption: The lease on the business location is assumable and has sufficient remaining term
assumptions.if_wrong: A landlord who refuses to assign the lease — or a lease expiring in 18 months — can kill a deal at close or create major post-close risk, especially for location-dependent businesses.
assumptions.how_to_check: Request the lease on day one of diligence. Confirm term, assignment clause, and landlord consent requirement. Lenders will also require this before funding.

assumptions.assumption: Key employees will stay through and after the transition
assumptions.if_wrong: In HVAC and services businesses, the lead technicians often are the business. Losing them post-close can destroy the revenue base the price was based on.
assumptions.how_to_check: During diligence, interview key employees (with seller permission). Structure seller transition period (90–180 days) and consider employee retention bonuses funded from the deal.

failure_patterns.pattern: Spending 6–12 months searching with no structured criteria and buying nothing
failure_patterns.seen_in: Multiple practitioner accounts in the source material describe buyers who spend half a year or more in unfocused search [S1, C3]
failure_patterns.avoid: Define your target criteria (geography, sector, revenue range, SDE floor) before you start. Build a broker outreach list in week one. Set a weekly activity metric (e.g., 5 new broker conversations per week).

failure_patterns.pattern: Paying too much because add-backs were not challenged
failure_patterns.seen_in: Quality of earnings diligence section [C7, S4] — sellers routinely inflate SDE with personal expenses that will not disappear post-close
failure_patterns.avoid: Commission a QoE report from an independent CPA before removing your diligence contingency. Apply a strict add-back test: does this expense genuinely disappear when the seller leaves? [C7]

failure_patterns.pattern: Modeling the deal without running the DSCR check, then losing lender approval
failure_patterns.seen_in: Valuation and deal calculator sources [C5, C9] — lenders apply a 1.25× DSCR floor that overrides any agreed-upon multiple
failure_patterns.avoid: Before making an offer, run the deal calculator with conservative SDE, your actual salary requirement, and current rate assumptions. If DSCR < 1.25×, the price is too high for SBA financing regardless of market comps [C5].

failure_patterns.pattern: No seller transition plan, leading to revenue loss in the first 90 days
failure_patterns.seen_in: Deal walkthrough sources emphasize seller transition as a frequently skipped step [C3, C8]
failure_patterns.avoid: Negotiate a defined transition period (minimum 90 days, ideally 6 months for owner-operator businesses) into the LOI and APA. Make it a condition of close, not an afterthought.

failure_patterns.pattern: Skipping professional advisors to save $10K–$20K, then losing far more
failure_patterns.seen_in: QoE report cost ($8K–$20K) is explicitly flagged as non-negotiable even on small deals [C7, S4]
failure_patterns.avoid: Budget for a buy-side attorney ($5K–$15K), a QoE CPA ($8K–$20K), and an SBA-experienced lender from the start. These are not optional costs — they are insurance against catastrophic mistakes.

analysis.verdict: The SBA 7(a) / seller note structure is the right tool for this goal, and the target sectors (HVAC, services, light manufacturing) are genuinely well-suited to it — the playbook is proven and the math can work. However, you are not yet ready to make an offer: your liquid capital position is unknown, you have no lender pre-qualification, and no broker relationships, which means the 12-month clock is already ticking against you. The single most valuable thing you can do in the next two weeks is get a hard number on your liquid capital, call three SBA preferred lenders for pre-qualification conversations, and define your target criteria in writing — everything else follows from those three actions.
